title: Notification Service
brief: Design a Notification Service that routes alerts to multiple configurable channels while keeping the core logic open to extension and decoupled from channel specifics.

requirements.text: Application code triggers a notification with a type and data payload.
Which channels a notification type goes to is supplied as configuration, not written into the service.
Each channel formats the notification content according to its own rules.
Adding a new channel does not require changes to existing notification logic.
Failure in one channel must not prevent other channels from delivering the notification.
The service is constructed with a configuration object; no global mutable state is used.

constraints: Configuration is supplied at construction; no global state
No actual network calls; mockable transports
Core service must not contain channel-specific logic

variationPoints.name: channel
variationPoints.why: Email, SMS, push, webhook and future channels

variationPoints.why: Plain text, HTML, JSON, etc. per channel

scenarios.title: The email channel throws; SMS still delivered
scenarios.description: The email channel throws an exception during send; SMS channel completes successfully and caller sees no error.

probes.prompt: How does your design know which channels a notification of a given type goes to? Is that a table the service is built with, or logic inside a class — and what has to change when a new type appears?

commonFailureModes.name: Hardcoded channel logic leads to brittle changes
commonFailureModes.description: Service contains switch-case for each channel, making new channel additions hard.

commonFailureModes.name: Single interface mixes sending and formatting
commonFailureModes.description: Channel interface requires both format and send methods, causing many stubs.

commonFailureModes.name: Failure in a channel stops all notifications
commonFailureModes.description: One channel throws and propagates, killing other deliveries.

assumptions: Which channels a type goes to is fixed at construction
A failed send is reported in the result, never thrown to the caller

strong.tradeoffs: Separating Channel and Formatter keeps channel logic extensible and decouples formatting rules. Returning a result type from Channel.send and aggregating it in NotificationService allows precise failure reporting and keeps the service loop simple.

decisions.alternative: A base class every channel extends
decisions.why: Any number of independent channel implementations without forcing inheritance

decisions.alternative: A switch on type inside the router
decisions.why: The mapping is configuration handed in at construction; the router never names a channel

decisions.what: Channel.send returns a SendResult instead of throwing
decisions.alternative: Let exceptions propagate and catch them in the router
decisions.why: A channel that reports rather than throws cannot stop the loop; the router keeps routing and reports every outcome together
Layouts are reused across channels and a new layout does not touch any channel

critiquePairs.question: A team wants alerts sent to Slack. Which design lets them add that without editing the class that routes notifications? Click the class they would implement.
critiquePairs.telling: In the strong design a Slack destination is one more implementation of Channel, registered in the ChannelRegistry the router is built with, so NotificationRouter is untouched. In the hardcoded design NotificationService names every channel it knows, so adding Slack means editing it.

critiquePairs.question: Both designs have a destination abstraction. In which one does a new destination NOT have to know how a message is laid out as text? Click the class that took that job away from destinations.
critiquePairs.telling: The strong design separates layout from sending: the Formatter interface, implemented by PlainTextFormatter and JsonFormatter, owns rendering, and a channel only sends. In the fat-interface design every channel must also format, so a new channel carries layout code it did not want.
